title: Counted loop
body:
Usually used with a [[For loop]]

```C++
while (counter <= 10){
	counter ++;
}
```

or

```c++
for (int counter = 1; counter <= 10; counter++) {
	// same loop, all three parts in one line
}
```

A loop that knows **how many** iterations it will do before it starts. The count comes from a
constant, a variable, or the size of an [[Array]]; either way it does not depend on what
happens inside the body.

The `for` header is the counted loop written down honestly: initialise, test, update, all in
one place where you can see whether they agree. Splitting them across a [[While loop]] is the
same loop and is easier to get wrong, because the update line can drift away from the test or
go missing entirely, which is an [[Infinite loop]].

The opposite is a [[Sentinel]] loop, which runs until it sees a stop value and cannot know the
count in advance. Choosing between them is question one of [[Loop design]]: do you know when to
stop, or do you have to be told?

Off by one is the standing hazard. `counter <= 10` starting at 1 runs ten times; starting at 0
it runs eleven. For arrays the form is always `for (i = 0; i < SIZE; i++)`, with `<` and not
`<=`; see [[Index]].
